newsitem.title: USA: ATHLETICS-SLANEY TO BE SUSPENDED FROM U.S. MEET.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-SLANEY TO BE SUSPENDED FROM U.S. MEET.

text.p: U.S. athletics officials said on Tuesday they would invalidate suspended runner Mary Slaney's entry into this week's national championships once they received formal notification of her suspension by the International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF).

The world governing body's secretary-general, Istvan Gyulai, said the notification had been faxed on Tuesday and that U.S. officials had been told to suspend Slaney if she is not cleared by an American hearing panel of a disputed doping test.

"They have been instructed to suspend her and to inform all the other athletes of her suspension," Gyulai said from IAAF headquarters in Monte Carlo. "She is prohibited from running nationally or internationally."

Asked about Gyulai's comments, USA Track & Field spokesman Pete Cava said when the notification was received "we will have to invalidate her entry" into the championships, which start here on Wednesday.
"We have to adhere to IAAF rules," Cava said.
Slaney's choices now will be either not to compete or to seek court action, arbitration, or relief from the United States Olympic Committee.
Slaney's husband, Richard, said from their home in Eugene, Oregon, that Mary had not decided what to do.
"They have to tell us that her entry is invalidated, then we will go from there," he said.

"But I can't imagine Mary wanting to seek a court order or go to arbitration. So what ... (if she wins a court order or arbitration) she runs and wins. Then so what. She would not be allowed to compete in the world championships."

Slaney's attorney, Jim Coleman, accused USA Track and Field of not protecting her rights and said the organisation "would be held accountable" under the U.S. Amateur Sports Act and the U.S. Olympic Committee's constitution. He would not specify what action he planned to take.

Slaney and fellow Americans Sandra Farmer-Patrick and Stephon Flenoy were suspended by the IAAF 10 days ago pending the outcome of U.S. hearings into drug tests last summer. In each case the athlete was found to have a higher than acceptable ratio of testerone to epi-testerone. Under IAAF rules, any ratio above 6-1 is considered suspicious and an athlete is subject to suspension.
Farmer-Patrick, a former U.S. women's 400-meter hurdles record holder, tried unsuccessfully on Monday to enter the U.S. championships.
She and Flenoy, a little-known hurdler, have been suspended by the U.S. federation. Slaney has not.

Farmer-Patrick was still pursuing ways on Tuesday to enter the championships. Flenoy has a U.S. Olympic Committee arbitration hearing scheduled for Wednesday. If successful, he would be permitted to run.
Slaney and Farmer-Patrick have denied taking any substance banned by the IAAF, but Gyulai said, "There is a very clear indication that this (Slaney) is a doping case."

Asked what would happen if the U.S. federation decided at some point to allow Slaney to compete, Gyulai said: "I don't believe any member of the IAAF can ignore the actions of the IAAF. There would be outrage."
Even if the U.S. federation clears Slaney, the IAAF would take the case to arbitration between the two federations, he said.
